claim.pdf_says: Headings '14.6.13.1.4   Nonfatal exception conditions' and '14.6.13.1.5   Exception objects' - fifth-level clause numbers, siblings of 14.6.13.1.1 'General'.
claim.markdown_says: Line 24237: '### 14.6.13.1.4 Nonfatal exception conditions'; line 24250: '### 14.6.13.1.5 Exception objects'
claim.why_it_matters: At '###' these two sit at the same depth as their parent 14.6.13.1 'Exception conditions' rather than one level below it, so the 14.6.13.1 subtree closes early in any generated outline. Sibling 14.6.13.1.1 is at '####'.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on four independent grounds. (1) Nothing is missing. The rendered PDF page 580 (printed folio 550) prints exactly two bold headings, '14.6.13.1.4 Nonfatal exception conditions' and '14.6.13.1.5 Exception objects'. Both appear in specs/ISO_COBOL.md verbatim, with the correct clause number and the correct title, each preceded by its correct anchor (, ). The whole page transcribes faithfully: the opening 'If checking is not enabled for a fatal exception condition...' paragraph, the .1.4 lead-in paragraph, all four numbered items 1)-4), the .1.5 lead-in 'When an exception object is raised, the following occurs:', both numbered items 1)-2), and the closing 'If an exception object is raised by a RAISE statement...' paragraph. Zero content loss. The classification 'missing-heading' is therefore wrong on its face -- the headings are present. (2) The alleged discrepancy is not a PDF-vs-markdown difference at all. The PDF has no markdown heading depth to lose: in the printed page the clause hierarchy is carried entirely by the dotted decimal number '14.6.13.1.4', and both headings are set in the identical bold face used for every other clause heading in this region, with no typographic size or indent distinction by level. The markdown reproduces those dotted numbers exactly. The '#' count is a transcription-side encoding choice, i.e. formatting -- explicitly one of the reject criteria. (3) The stated consequence is factually wrong. The outline does NOT 'close early' at 14.6.13.1.4. The two immediately preceding siblings are SHALLOWER than the ones complained about: line 24190 is '## 14.6.13.1.2 Normal completion of a declarative procedure' and line 24206 is '## 14.6.13.1.3 Fatal exception conditions', both at '##'. Any generated outline therefore already terminated the 14.6.13.1 subtree ~50 lines earlier, at .1.2. Relative to its own predecessors, '### 14.6.13.1.4' is one level DEEPER, not the break point. The claim isolates .1.4/.1.5 as the defect when they are in fact the least anomalous members of the run. (4) Both quoted line numbers are wrong. The headings are at lines 24240 and 24253, not 24237 and 24250. The claim's supporting premise is also only half true: '14.6.13.1.1 General' occurs TWICE in the file -- at line 24107 as '## 14.6.13.1.1' and at line 24148 as '#### 14.6.13.1.1' -- because the block 14.6.13 / 14.6.13.1 / 14.6.13.1.1 is duplicated (24101-24107 all at '##', then re-emitted at 24142-24148 as '##' / '###' / '####'). Citing '14.6.13.1.1 is at ####' as the reference depth silently picks one of two conflicting copies. What is genuinely true is only this: heading-level assignment across the whole 14.6.13 region of the transcription is inconsistent ('##' for .1.1/.1.2/.1.3, '###' for .1.4/.1.5/.1.6, plus a duplicated parent block). That is a pre-existing, file-wide markdown-structure artifact spanning pages 575-580, not a page-580 content discrepancy against the PDF, and it is not what this finding describes.
